case_study_insert.main_stem: Caldbeck Lime Works (CLW) is a partnership in the eco-materials and construction-materials sector, burning high-calcium lime for conservation mortars, plasters and limewash used by restoration contractors. Founded in 2009 by Harriet and Joe Callis, it employs a workforce of 33 and operates a flat organisational structure with laissez-faire leadership that trusts its experienced kiln burners. CLW plans to invest $520,000 in a new kiln with waste-heat recovery to cut fuel use and emissions, financed by a $320,000 bank loan and $200,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $168,000 a year, a variable cost of $8.40 a unit and a selling price of $14.40, and currently produces 40,000 units a year. Its kiln batch defect rate has reached 4.7%, wasting fuel and forcing expensive reburning.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — October 2025: The kiln produced 10,000 units of quicklime and hot-mix mortar last quarter; 4.7% of batches failed calcium-purity testing, up from 3.2% a year ago, and reburning consumed an extra 61 tonnes of gas. Average order fulfilment is 6 days. Market research of 280 conservation contractors found that 62% would pay a 5% premium for certified high-calcium lime with chain-of-custody paperwork, and 54% rank consistent batch purity as decisive. A loader breakdown log shows 7 stoppages last quarter; off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $850 per employee, while on-the-job training relies on senior burners and is uncertified, and 11 of 33 staff lack hot-mix handling certification.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Caldbeck Lime Works for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, its third rise this year, increasing variable-rate loan costs. (2) Industrial gas prices paid by medium manufacturers rose 14.9% year-on-year, the fourth consecutive quarterly increase, while home insulation retrofit grants for older buildings rose by $1,000. (3) The national minimum wage will rise by 1.5% to $11.70 per hour from April 2026, and construction-sector input inflation stands at 5.2%.

questions.question_text: CLW plans to finance part of its waste-heat recovery kiln with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for CLW of using retained profit to fund the kiln instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs CLW no interest or arrangement fees, protecting cash when fixed costs already run at $168,000 a year. The central bank has raised its base rate from 4.75% to 5.25%, so variable-rate borrowing keeps getting more expensive; funding $200,000 internally avoids that exposure and preserves the $8.40 variable-cost cushion on 40,000 units of lime. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices without weakening the $14.40 selling price that conservation contractors accept for certified high-calcium lime.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps full ownership and control with Harriet and Joe Callis as the two partners. No lender can impose covenants on kiln scheduling, staffing across the flat laissez-faire structure, or how the new kiln is commissioned. It also avoids collateral risk against the kiln itself if the 4.7% batch defect rate persisted and reburning kept consuming an extra 61 tonnes of gas, and it avoids diluting the partnership's simple structure — no share issue, no community investors, no outside shareholder expectations for dividends if a quarter's profits are retained to weather fuel-price volatility.

Quality of finance: Using $200,000 retained profit for part of the $520,000 package means the bank loan covers only $320,000, keeping annual repayments well within the cash generated at 40,000 units of output and matched against the 5% premium the 62% of surveyed contractors already signal.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Caldbeck Lime Works and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: CLW is launching certified high-calcium lime for conservation work. Consider specialist trade magazine print advertising, free lime-plastering workshops for contractors, or social media restoration case studies. Which should CLW choose to promote the lime? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Specialist trade magazine print advertising: Advertising in conservation and building-restoration titles reaches exactly the 280 conservation contractors surveyed, who rely on technical copy for mortar specifications and whose trust carries into specification decisions. Magazines allow detailed claims about 4.7% batch purity improvement, chain-of-custody paperwork and the 5% certified premium, and suit a slow-moving, high-trust purchase. Drawbacks: circulation in this niche is small, younger specifiers rarely read print, and response cannot be measured beyond coupon or QR codes — reach outside the existing subscriber base is minimal.

Free lime-plastering workshops: Half-day workshops at CLW's kiln yard teach contractors hot-mix practice, correct curing and the paperwork auditors expect, directly converting 62% of the 280 contractors willing to pay a 5% premium into confident specifiers while positioning CLW as the technical authority. Costs are materials and time, and every attendee leaves able to promote hot-mix work on their own sites — powerful word-of-mouth in a tight-knit restoration community. Drawbacks: limited attendee numbers per session, risk of teaching rivals' clients, and no guarantee of immediate orders after one workshop.

Social media restoration case studies: Short videos of real limewash and mortar projects show visual before/after results and reach younger site managers cheaply, and can be targeted at conservation hashtags and followers of heritage bodies. Drawbacks: the audience is broad and low-intent — most viewers will never specify high-calcium lime — and algorithm reach is unreliable; technical credibility arguments about purity and certification are weak in a fifteen-second clip.

Recommendation: CLW should choose free lime-plastering workshops. They deliver the highest-quality engagement per dollar spent: attendees experience the 14.9% fuel-cost story and the certified quality hands-on, turning the 54% who rank batch purity as decisive into loyal specifiers. Trade magazine print is rejected as too narrow and unmeasurable to justify sustained spend; social media case studies are rejected as low-intent reach that cannot carry the technical trust required for conservation specification. Workshops also generate content that feeds social channels for free, so print remains optional for a few flagship issues rather than the core campaign.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CLW with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CLW with a well-justified recommendation explaining why print advertising and social media case studies are rejected.

questions.question_text: CLW's kiln batch defect rate has reached 4.7%. Explain two benefits for CLW of using laissez-faire leadership to keep its experienced kiln burners and mill crews motivated.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership trusts CLW's experienced kiln burners to set firing curves, loading sequences and quenching timing themselves, exploiting their deep craft knowledge far better than rigid rules would. Giving them this autonomy satisfies higher-level esteem and self-actualisation needs, lifts job satisfaction and cuts the supervision headcount a flat partnership of 33 staff can afford. Burners with genuine ownership of the kiln experiment with small loading and fuel-mix changes that directly attack the 4.7% batch defect rate and the wasted 61 tonnes of gas — practical innovation management cannot dictate from above.

Point 2: When crews are trusted rather than monitored, morale improves and absenteeism and turnover fall — vital for a rural kiln employing skilled staff who are hard to replace. Laissez-faire oversight also shortens the chain of command between the partners and the mill floor, so a burner who spots an impure limestone batch can halt the feed immediately, protecting the 40,000 units of annual production and the 6 days fulfilment promise that contractors rely on for scheduled restoration scaffolding. Motivation built on trust, not fear, is also cheaper than financial incentives in a cash-tight year of gas-price inflation.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CLW's kiln defects, workforce and output.

questions.question_text: Eleven of CLW's 33 staff lack hot-mix handling certification. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at $850 per employee. Which should CLW choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Showing the 11 uncertified staff hot-mix practice at the kiln keeps them productive while learning CLW's own batch timings, mortar consistencies and loading sequences, costs nothing in fees, and builds machine-specific habits under trusted senior burners. Drawbacks: senior burners lose firing time, bad habits pass from burner to burner, and — critically — on-the-job training is uncertified, so CLW has no document insurers or heritage auditors will accept. Calcium-hot-lime burns skin and eyes in seconds; after the reburning waste already recorded, another burn incident would force shutdown and liability review.

Off-the-job training: The college hot-mix handling course at $850 per employee gives structured, accredited certification in hot-mix safety, mortar chemistry, PPE and emergency response, costing $9,350 in total — easily affordable against a $520,000 kiln investment and one bad incident avoided. Drawbacks: 11 staff leave the kiln for a day or two, the syllabus is generic rather than Caldbeck-specific, and travel to the college cuts into dispatch weeks.

Decision: CLW should choose off-the-job training. Hot-mix lime is a burn hazard that insurers and heritage clients must see certified, and uncertified crews cannot handle hot-mix deliveries at all once contracts harden certification requirements — a risk no amount of on-site mentoring removes. The $9,350 fee is recovered if it prevents even one reburning event or delivery refusal. On-the-job training is rejected as the primary route because it is uncertified and cannot reduce CLW's insurer risk; it remains useful only as short refresher sessions at the kiln after the certificate is in place.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CLW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of CLW.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of CLW with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, certification and safety.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CLW's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $168,000 ÷ ($14.40 − $8.40) = $168,000 ÷ $6.00 = 28,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 28,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $14.40 − $8.40 = $6.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $6.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CLW's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. CLW's managers can compare the 28,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 40,000 units, confirming a margin of safety of 12,000 units before the new waste-heat recovery kiln adds capacity and higher fixed costs.
2. Contribution per unit of $6.00 lets managers model the 5% certified premium the 62% of surveyed contractors support; a price of $15.12 would lift contribution to $6.72, testing whether the premium is self-funding.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $168,000 and contribution per unit lets managers check the new kiln can service the $320,000 bank loan from first-year cash flows and stress-test the effect of the 14.9% gas-price rise recurring.
4. Unit cost data ($168,000 ÷ 40,000 units + $8.40 = $12.60 a unit) lets managers benchmark each quarter, target the 4.7% batch defect rate causing reburning of an extra 61 tonnes of gas, and renegotiate the $8.40 variable cost with kiln-fuel suppliers.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 28,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $6.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 12,000 units at 40,000 units output; 5% premium-pricing modelling at $15.12; $320,000 loan-service feasibility under a 14.9% gas-price rise; and unit-cost benchmarking at $12.60 to attack the 4.7% batch defect rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CLW's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has CLW's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 36.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 8.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 12.0%
ROCE 2024 = 11.0%
ROCE 2025 = 15.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue rose from $3,850,000 to $4,400,000 while cost of sales grew only from $2,464,000 to $2,640,000, so the trading surplus widened to $1,386,000 and then $1,760,000. Operating profit moved from $308,000 on sales of $3,850,000 to $528,000 on sales of $4,400,000. Capital employed grew from $2,800,000 to $3,520,000 as the kiln project was funded, and interest payable rose from $140,000 to $165,000.

Evaluation: Performance strengthened across every measure. The share of revenue kept after production costs widened from 36.0% to 40.0%, reflecting better high-calcium certified mixes, tighter batch discipline and chain-of-custody paperwork that qualifies the 5% premium the 62% of contractors accept. The surplus after operating costs improved from $308,000 to $528,000, and the return earned on the enlarged capital base rose from 11.0% to 15.0%, so the kiln investment is already out-earning its funding cost. Caution is warranted: capital employed grew by $720,000, reburning still consumed an extra 61 tonnes of gas, and interest payable rose to $165,000 alongside the $320,000 loan — so any slip in the 4.7% defect rate would compress returns quickly in a year of 14.9% gas inflation.

Conclusion: CLW's financial position has improved. Trading margins and returns on the capital base all moved favourably, and the improvement is rooted in genuine premium pricing and waste reduction rather than accounting effects. The partners should commission the new waste-heat recovery kiln promptly, protect the certified batch discipline that underpins the 40.0% surplus share, and refinance the bank loan if rates rise further.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements and a justified conclusion on whether CLW's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CLW of adopting the waste-heat recovery kiln to produce lower-carbon lime.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Waste-heat recovery recaptures exhaust heat to pre-dry and pre-heat incoming limestone, cutting the fuel burned per unit of lime and directly reducing exposure to the 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices. It also cuts CLW's emissions per unit, letting the partners claim verified lower-carbon lime — a claim the 62% of surveyed contractors willing to pay a 5% premium for certified product would value, and one that strengthens chain-of-custody paperwork demanded by heritage bodies specifying for listed buildings.

Disadvantage: The $520,000 kiln is a large capital commitment for a $3,520,000-capital-employed partnership, and installation requires weeks of shutdown. During installation, average order fulfilment slips beyond the current 6 days, jeopardising the 54% of contractors who rank consistent supply as decisive and risking contract penalties on scheduled restoration scaffolding. If the heat-recovery system underperforms, fuel savings may be lower than modelled, squeezing the $8.40 variable cost exactly when gas prices have risen 14.9%.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CLW's research data, fuel costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices and the 1.5% minimum wage increase will affect CLW. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.75% to 5.25%): If CLW's $320,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.5 percentage-point rise adds about $1,600 a year of interest — modest against fixed costs of $168,000. Higher rates also cool construction lending, which could slow the wider restoration pipeline that drives demand for conservation lime, and raise the cost of refinancing when the loan is renewed. CLW can fix or hedge; the direct cash impact is small.

Minimum wage increase (1.5% to $11.70): With 33 staff, mainly kiln burners, loader drivers and mill crew, a 1.5% rise adds roughly $11,400 a year if all staff earn near the current rate (33 × $23,050 × 1.5% ≈ $11,400) — meaningful but absorbable through batch discipline gains and the 5% certified premium. It ranks behind the fuel problem in urgency.

Industrial gas price rise (14.9%): The kiln is CLW's biggest cost engine. Gas already forced reburning of an extra 61 tonnes last quarter at a 4.7% defect rate. If fuel is roughly 30% of the $8.40 variable cost (≈ $2.52), a 14.9% rise adds about $0.38 per unit — roughly $15,100 a year on 40,000 units, before any reburning multiplier on faulty batches. Unlike wages and interest, this cost scales with every unit produced and cannot be renegotiated away without the waste-heat recovery kiln.

Conclusion: The 14.9% rise in industrial gas prices will have the greatest impact. It is the largest percentage increase on CLW's biggest production cost, it compounds with the 4.7% defect rate into reburning waste, and it applies to every one of the 40,000 units sold — totalling roughly $15,000 a year before reburning, several times the interest-rate impact ($1,600) and comfortably above the 1.5% wage rise (around $11,400). CLW must commission the waste-heat recovery kiln quickly, lock fuel contracts with suppliers, and pass part of the increase into the certified 5% premium before taking on new restoration orders.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CLW.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CLW's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CLW with a well-justified judgement that the gas-price rise has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
